title: Why Some 911 Calls Reached the Wrong Center #shorts
summary: Wireless 911 calls were routed by the tower that handled them; an industry body estimated about 12% were misrouted. Since 2024 the FCC requires routing by the phone's location when it is known within 165 meters.
sources: Wireless 911 calls have historically been routed by the location of the cell tower that handles the call; ATIS estimates that on average 12% of wireless legacy E911 voice calls are misrouted; location-based routing is required when the caller's location is known within 165 meters at 90% confidence (nationwide carriers within 6 months, rules effective 13 May 2024); device-based hybrid location uses crowd-sourced Wi-Fi, A-GNSS and other handset sensors (FCC Report and Order, Location-Based Routing for Wireless 911 Calls, Federal Register, 13 Mar 2024): https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-03-13/html/2024-03157.htm

scenes.narration: By one industry estimate, about {12%|twelve percent} of cell calls to {911|nine one one} landed at the wrong center.
Because calls were routed by the tower they reached, not by where the caller stood.
In {2024|twenty twenty-four}, the FCC told carriers to route by the phone's location, when it's known within {165|a hundred sixty-five} meters.
The tower used to decide. Now, when it can, the phone does.
